_about: Verified law cards. The model may ONLY cite these, by ID. Every card was checked against the linked source on the 'verified' date. Add a card = add a law the bot is allowed to talk about.

cards.title: Free legal aid (Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, s.12)
cards.text: Free legal services (a lawyer, advice, drafting) are available to: women and children, members of Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, industrial workmen, persons with disability, victims of trafficking or disaster, people in custody, and anyone whose income is below the limit set by their state. Apply at the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court, online at nalsa.gov.in, or call the NALSA helpline 15100 (toll-free).

cards.title: Lok Adalat / pre-litigation settlement (Legal Services Authorities Act, s.19)
cards.text: Legal Services Authorities organise Lok Adalats where a dispute can be settled by agreement, even before a case is filed. There is no court fee. Ask at the DLSA or call 15100.

cards.title: Time limit for civil money-recovery cases (Limitation Act, 1963)
cards.text: Most civil suits to recover money must be filed within 3 years. When the 3 years start depends on the facts (for example, when the money became due or was refused). If you are close to 3 years, talk to a lawyer quickly.

cards.title: New criminal laws from 1 July 2024
cards.text: From 1 July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), the CrPC by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and the Evidence Act by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA). Old IPC/CrPC section numbers do not apply to new incidents. Criminal matters need a lawyer.

cards.title: Security deposit under the Model Tenancy Act, 2021 (s.11)
cards.text: The Model Tenancy Act caps the security deposit at 2 months' rent for homes (6 months for non-residential) and says it is to be refunded when the landlord takes back vacant possession, after lawful deductions. It is a MODEL law: it applies only where a state has adopted it or passed a similar law (a few states, e.g. Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Assam have tenancy laws on these lines). Elsewhere your rent agreement and the state's rent law decide.

cards.title: Normal wear and tear (Transfer of Property Act, s.108(m))
cards.text: A tenant must return the property in the condition they received it, EXCEPT for reasonable wear and tear. So routine repainting, faded walls or normal ageing usually cannot be charged to the tenant unless the agreement clearly says otherwise; real damage can be.

cards.title: Compensation for breach of contract (Indian Contract Act, s.73)
cards.text: If someone breaks a contract (like a rent agreement that promises the deposit back), the other side can claim compensation for the loss that naturally follows from the breach.

cards.title: Where to file for a deposit not returned
cards.text: Usual path: written demand -> legal notice -> case. If your state has a Rent Authority / Rent Court under its tenancy law, go there. Otherwise file a civil suit for recovery of money in the civil court (Small Causes Court in some cities). Where there is a written agreement for a fixed sum, a lawyer may use the faster summary-suit procedure under Order XXXVII of the Code of Civil Procedure. Court fees and the right court depend on the state and the amount - a lawyer or the DLSA can confirm.

cards.title: Who is a consumer; defect and deficiency (Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s.2)
cards.text: You are a 'consumer' if you bought goods or hired a service for your own use (not for resale/commercial purpose), including online purchases. A faulty product is a 'defect'; poor or incomplete service (like a refund promised but not paid) is a 'deficiency'. Both can be taken to a Consumer Commission.

cards.title: Which Consumer Commission and where (s.34, s.35 + 2021 Jurisdiction Rules)
cards.text: District Commission: value paid up to Rs 50 lakh. State Commission: above Rs 50 lakh up to Rs 2 crore. National Commission: above Rs 2 crore. The value is what you PAID, not what you claim. You can file in the district where you live or work, and you can file it yourself without a lawyer.

cards.title: Online filing on e-Jagriti and fees
cards.text: Consumer complaints can be filed online at https://e-jagriti.gov.in (it replaced e-Daakhil in January 2025). For the District Commission there is no fee when the value paid is up to Rs 5 lakh; small fees apply above that.

cards.title: 2-year time limit for consumer complaints (s.69)
cards.text: A consumer complaint must be filed within 2 years from the date the problem (cause of action) arose. A late complaint is accepted only if the Commission is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay and records its reasons.

cards.title: What the Commission can order (s.39)
cards.text: The Commission can order the seller/service provider to repair or replace the product, refund the price, pay compensation for loss or harassment, stop an unfair practice, and pay litigation costs.

cards.title: National Consumer Helpline 1915 (free, before going to court)
cards.text: Call 1915 or file at consumerhelpline.gov.in. The helpline takes up your grievance with the company for free. It cannot pass binding orders, but many refunds get resolved here. Keep the docket number as evidence.

cards.title: E-commerce grievance officer (E-Commerce Rules, 2020)
cards.text: Online marketplaces and sellers must have a grievance officer whose contact is shown on the platform. The officer must acknowledge your complaint within 48 hours and resolve it within one month.

cards.title: Code on Wages, 2019 is now the law on wages
cards.text: The Code on Wages, 2019 came into force on 21 November 2025. It replaced the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. It applies to employees of all establishments.

cards.title: Deadline to pay wages (Code on Wages, s.17)
cards.text: Monthly wages must be paid before the 7th day of the next month (weekly: last working day of the week; daily: end of shift). If an employee resigns, is removed, dismissed or retrenched, or the establishment closes, wages due must be paid within 2 working days.

cards.title: Filing a wage claim (Code on Wages, s.45)
cards.text: An employee (or their registered trade union, or the Inspector-cum-Facilitator) can file a claim for unpaid or short-paid wages before the authority appointed by the government (usually through the state Labour Department). The claim should be filed within 3 years of the date it arose; later claims are allowed only for sufficient cause. Several workers can file one joint claim. Note: people in senior managerial roles should confirm with a lawyer whether this route or a civil suit fits them.

cards.title: Cheque bounce is an offence (NI Act, s.138)
cards.text: If a cheque given to pay a legally owed debt bounces for insufficient funds, the payee must send a written demand notice within 30 days of getting the bank's return memo. If the drawer pays within 15 days of receiving the notice, no offence is made out. If not, it is an offence punishable with up to 2 years' jail, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both.

cards.title: Deadline to file the cheque bounce complaint (NI Act, s.142)
cards.text: The complaint must be filed before the Magistrate within one month after the 15-day payment period ends. Courts can accept a late complaint only if sufficient cause for delay is shown; the Supreme Court has treated this limit as strict.

cards.title: Interim compensation (NI Act, s.143A)
cards.text: During a cheque bounce trial the court may order the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount to the complainant.

cards.title: What counts as domestic violence and who can use the DV Act (s.2, s.3)
cards.text: Domestic violence covers physical abuse (beating, slapping, causing injury), sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse (insults, threats, taunts about dowry or not having a son) and economic abuse (stopping money for household needs, taking her salary or stridhan, throwing her out). Any woman in a domestic relationship can use it: a wife, a woman in a live-in relationship in the nature of marriage, a mother, sister or daughter living in the same house. She can name the husband and his relatives (for example in-laws) as respondents.

cards.title: How to start a DV case: Protection Officer and application to the Magistrate (s.9, s.12, s.27)
cards.text: She (or the Protection Officer, or someone on her behalf) files an application under s.12 before the Judicial Magistrate. Every district has a Protection Officer (s.9) who records a Domestic Incident Report, helps her file, and arranges medical help and shelter, free of cost. She can file in the court where she now lives, even temporarily (for example at her parents' home), or where the husband lives, or where the violence happened (s.27). The Magistrate should ordinarily fix the first hearing within 3 days of receiving the application and try to decide it within 60 days of the first hearing (s.12).

cards.title: What the Magistrate can order (s.17-22)
cards.text: Protection order (s.18): stop the violence, stop contact, stop entering her workplace, stop selling joint assets. Right to live in the shared household (s.17) and residence order (s.19): she cannot be thrown out of the matrimonial home; the court can remove the abuser from it or order alternative housing and the return of her stridhan and valuables. Monetary relief (s.20): medical expenses, lost earnings, damaged property and maintenance for her and her children. Custody of children (s.21). Compensation (s.22) for injuries and mental torture and emotional distress.

cards.title: Urgent (ex parte) orders and breach (s.23, s.31)
cards.text: If she is in danger, the Magistrate can pass an interim or ex parte protection order on her affidavit itself, without first hearing the husband (s.23). Breaking a protection order is a criminal offence: up to 1 year in jail, or fine up to Rs 20,000, or both (s.31), and she can call the police when it is broken.

cards.title: Cruelty by husband or in-laws is a crime (BNS s.85, s.86; earlier IPC 498A)
cards.text: A husband or his relative who subjects a woman to cruelty can be jailed up to 3 years and fined (BNS s.85). Cruelty (s.86) means wilful conduct likely to drive her to suicide or cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb or health (physical or mental), or harassment to force her or her family to meet an unlawful demand such as dowry. This replaced IPC 498A for incidents from 1 July 2024. Note: under Supreme Court directions (2025), a complaint only of this kind may first go to a district Family Welfare Committee, with no arrest for 2 months; this does not stop her DV Act case or her protection.

cards.title: Hurt and grievous hurt (BNS s.115-117)
cards.text: Voluntarily causing hurt (pain or injury) is punishable with up to 1 year, or fine up to Rs 10,000, or both (s.115). Grievous hurt (s.116) includes permanent disfigurement of the head or face, a fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth, and injury causing severe pain or inability to carry on normal work for 15 days. Voluntarily causing grievous hurt: up to 7 years and fine (s.117). Permanent scars on the face or head can count as grievous hurt; the doctor's medical report decides how the injury is classified.

cards.title: Filing an FIR: any police station, e-FIR, free copy, if police refuse (BNSS s.173)
cards.text: An FIR for a cognizable offence can be filed at ANY police station, even if the incident happened elsewhere (Zero FIR); it is then transferred. Information can also be given electronically (e-FIR) and must be signed at the station within 3 days. The complainant gets a free copy of the FIR. For offences punishable with 3 to 7 years, the police may, with a senior officer's permission, first hold a preliminary enquiry of up to 14 days (s.173(3)). If the police refuse to register the FIR, the complaint can be sent in writing to the Superintendent of Police (s.173(4)).

cards.title: Maintenance for wife and children (BNSS s.144; earlier CrPC 125)
cards.text: A wife who cannot maintain herself, and children, can ask the Magistrate to order the husband to pay monthly maintenance if he has means and neglects or refuses to support them. This is separate from, and can run alongside, monetary relief under the DV Act.

cards.title: One Stop Centre (Sakhi) and Women Helpline 181
cards.text: Women Helpline 181 is free and 24x7 and connects her to the district One Stop Centre (Sakhi), which gives under one roof, free: medical help and medico-legal examination, help with the police and FIR, free legal aid through the Legal Services Authority, counselling, and temporary shelter (usually up to 5 days). For immediate danger, 112.

cards.title: Extortion, and threats made in order to extort (BNS s.308)
cards.text: Extortion (s.308(1)) has three ingredients: (1) the accused intentionally puts a person in fear of any injury to that person or to someone else; (2) thereby dishonestly induces the person; (3) to deliver property, money or a valuable security. 'Injury' means any harm illegally caused to a person in body, mind, reputation or property (s.2(14)), so a threat to publish private photos or damaging material counts. Illustration (a) to s.308: threatening to publish a defamatory libel unless paid money is extortion. Punishment: completed extortion - up to 7 years, or fine, or both (s.308(2)). Where nothing has yet been handed over, putting or attempting to put a person in fear of injury in order to commit extortion is itself punishable - up to 2 years, or fine, or both (s.308(3)); if the fear is of death or grievous hurt, up to 7 years and fine (s.308(4)). Extortion is a cognizable offence. These replace IPC ss.383-389 for acts from 1 July 2024.
cards.source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/ (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s.308); bare text: https://devgan.in/bns/section/308/

cards.title: Criminal intimidation (BNS s.351)
cards.text: Criminal intimidation (s.351(1)): threatening another by any means (including messages and calls) with injury to their person, reputation or property, or to someone they care about, with intent to cause them alarm, or to make them do something they are not legally bound to do, or stop doing something they are entitled to do. The intent must appear from the material (the words used, the context, any demand). Punishment: up to 2 years, or fine, or both (s.351(2)). If the threat is to cause death or grievous hurt, to destroy property by fire, to cause an offence punishable with 7 years or more, or to impute unchastity to a woman: up to 7 years, or fine, or both (s.351(3)). If done by anonymous communication or while hiding identity: up to 2 more years (s.351(4)). Simple criminal intimidation is non-cognizable and bailable. Replaces IPC ss.503, 506, 507.
cards.source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/ (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s.351); bare text: https://devgan.in/bns/section/351/

cards.title: Defamation (BNS s.356)
cards.text: Defamation (s.356(1)): making or publishing an imputation about a person, by words, signs or visible representations, intending to harm or knowing it will likely harm their reputation, subject to exceptions such as true statements made for the public good. Punishment: simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both, or community service (s.356(2)). It is taken up on a complaint by the person defamed to a Magistrate, not by the police on their own. A civil suit for damages and an injunction is a separate remedy.

cards.title: Voyeurism and stalking, where the victim is a woman (BNS s.77, s.78)
cards.text: Voyeurism (s.77): watching or capturing the image of a woman engaged in a private act where she would expect not to be observed, or disseminating such an image. If she consented to the image being taken but not to its being shared, sharing it is still an offence (Explanation 2). Punishment: first conviction 1 to 3 years and fine; later conviction 3 to 7 years and fine. Stalking (s.78): a man who repeatedly follows or contacts a woman to foster personal interaction despite her clear disinterest, or who monitors her use of the internet, email or other electronic communication. Punishment: first conviction up to 3 years and fine; later conviction up to 5 years and fine. Replace IPC ss.354C and 354D.

cards.title: Private and sexual images online (IT Act, s.66E, s.67, s.67A)
cards.text: Intentionally or knowingly capturing, publishing or transmitting an image of a private area of any person without their consent: up to 3 years, or fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or both (s.66E). Publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form: first conviction up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh (s.67). Publishing or transmitting material containing a sexually explicit act: first conviction up to 5 years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh (s.67A). These apply whatever the victim's gender, and cover sending to even one person by WhatsApp, email or social media.

cards.title: Platforms must take down intimate or morphed images within 24 hours of a complaint (IT Rules, 2021, rule 3(2)(b))
cards.text: Under rule 3(2)(b) of the IT Rules, 2021, a platform (WhatsApp, Instagram, X, a website host, etc.) must, within 24 hours of a complaint by the person or someone on their behalf, take all reasonable steps to remove or disable content that prima facie exposes their private area, shows them in full or partial nudity or in a sexual act, or impersonates them, including artificially morphed images. Complain through the platform's grievance officer / reporting form and keep the acknowledgement; a 2025 government SOP also routes such complaints through cybercrime.gov.in and One Stop Centres.

cards.title: WhatsApp chats, screenshots and recordings as evidence (BSA s.61, s.63)
cards.text: An electronic record cannot be refused as evidence merely because it is electronic (s.61). The original device on which a chat or recording is stored (your phone) is primary evidence. A copy - printout, screenshot, pen drive, CD - is admissible when it comes with a certificate in the form in the Schedule (s.63(4)): Part A signed by the person producing it, giving the device details and the hash value of the record, and Part B signed by an expert. The Supreme Court upheld this requirement in May 2026 and said Part B can be signed by any person with expertise in computer science or cyber forensics. So: keep the original phone, don't delete or edit the chat, export the full chat with media, and note numbers, handles, dates and URLs.
cards.source: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/ (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, ss.61, 63 and Schedule); https://www.livelaw.in/top-stories/supreme-court-rejects-challenge-to-s634-bsa-mandating-hash-value-disclosure-for-electronic-evidence-535950

cards.title: Reporting online threats: cybercrime.gov.in and helpline 1930
cards.text: Online threats, blackmail and the sharing of private images can be reported on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, cybercrime.gov.in (crimes against women and children can be reported there anonymously). If money was paid or taken online, call 1930 at once: quick reporting improves the chance of freezing it. A complaint at a police station or an e-FIR is a separate route and can be used at the same time.
